body.text: Taiwan’s 2026 local elections are in the final stages of campaigning, with just one week until the vote. What are the key races to keep an eye on in what has proved to be a surprising election full of ups and downs? And what will the implications be going forward?

The Taipei mayoral race has dominated national and international discussions of the local elections so far. Taiwan’s capital always attracts attention, but this year even more so due to the rise of Puma Shen as a competitive mayoral candidate for the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in a city that otherwise historically leans pan-Blue. Shen has distinguished himself with strong public speaking skills and a seemingly encyclopedic knowledge of policy.

In a race that should by all accounts lean in his favor, incumbent Chiang Wan-an of the Kuomintang (KMT) is on the defensive, at least in terms of public visibility. Scandals such as a raid on a Taipei gay bar shortly before Taiwan’s annual pride parade at the end of October, or criticisms of his mayoral administration for reducing the amount of greenery in Taipei, have not helped Chiang.

Even if Shen loses, he is on track to be the best-performing DPP candidate in Taipei since Chen Shui-bian, who won the mayoral election in 1994. Chen then went on to become the first DPP candidate elected to the presidency.

Shen now seems sure to have a continued political future – something that was previously uncertain for the one-term legislator, who was previously primarily known for a strong stance on China. Likewise, the incredible amount of public enthusiasm around Shen’s candidacy – dubbed the “Ocean Current” phenomenon – has proven large enough to impact other races across Taiwan, giving the DPP a boost nationwide.

On the other hand, Chiang Wan-an was previously thought to have ambitions to run for president as the KMT’s candidate in 2028, but his chances may have receded as he has struggled to fend off Shen. Naming Taichung mayor Lu Shiow-yen as his campaign chair was implicitly a signal that Chiang would be willing to step aside in favor of Lu in 2028 if she supports him in the present race.
Taichung

The Taichung mayoral race is also important to keep in focus. Not only is Taichung Taiwan’s second-largest city, as the main metropolis of central Taiwan, but the race will be an important one precisely because outgoing mayor Lu Shiow-yen of the KMT is expected to seek the 2028 presidential nomination.

DPP candidates have been able to win Taichung in the past, most recently with Lin Chia-lung from 2014 to 2018. Nevertheless, Ho Hsin-chun of the DPP is the underdog against former KMT chair Johnny Chiang, in a race that has often centered on issues of transportation infrastructure and how to boost Taichung’s visibility as a city on the international stage.

Chiang (no relation to Chiang Wan-an) is Lu’s anointed successor, but he has a strong standing in his own right, as a younger member of the KMT who has nonetheless held high positions in the party. It would be an upset if he were defeated – or, in fact, if he does not get more than 60 percent of the vote. If that were to occur, questions would be raised about Lu’s record in Taichung in such a way that would negatively impact her future presidential bid.
Kaohsiung
The southern metropolis of Kaohsiung, Taiwan’s third-largest city, is another election involving succession issues in what should be a safe election – this time for the DPP.

Lai Jui-lung is the anointed successor of outgoing DPP mayor Chen Chi-mai, who has been highly popular in spite of initially losing his 2020 mayoral bid to Han Kuo-yu of the KMT. Yet Lai has difficulty achieving recognition – one of his best-performing campaign ads, in fact, pointed fun at his own lack of recognizability.

Lai is up against veteran KMT legislator Ko Chih-en, who has been aggressive in attacks on the DPP’s record in Kaohsiung, alleging that the DPP has acted primarily in the interests of partisan politics and not to help the citizenry.

Han showed in 2020 that it is possible for the KMT to make inroads into the DPP’s traditional heartland of southern Taiwan. The KMT has tried to repeat that success since then. It is unclear whether Ko has enough local standing to sway the Kaohsiung race, but Lai is perhaps a weaker candidate than the DPP would have hoped for, and Kaohsiung is a city with many public sector workers – a population that has historically voted for the KMT.
New Taipei

The opposite dynamic, however, is at work in New Taipei, Taiwan’s largest city. Lee Shu-chuan of the KMT aims to inherit the reins from outgoing mayor Hou You-yi, who served as the KMT’s 2024 presidential candidate. However, though Lee – by training, a civil engineer – is known as a competent administrator, he has proven poor at campaigning and has struggled to articulate a distinctive policy platform.

Consequently, Su Chiao-hui of the DPP, a more experienced politician and the daughter of former premier Su Tseng-chang, has proven unexpectedly successful in campaigning against Lee. Even before Shen’s “Ocean Current” effect – whose influence is probably strongest in the greater Taipei metropolitan area – had begun to impact races across Taiwan, Su had already been successful in narrowing the gap between her and Lee.

Even if Shen ultimately is defeated in Taipei, it is possible that New Taipei is won by the DPP. If so, much like the “Han wave” that washed over Kaohsiung in 2020, national political discourse would question whether the KMT was losing its traditional power base in northern Taiwan, with the successes of the DPP in winning over swing voters and young people.
Other Local Races and Party Dynamics

Besides major metropolitan areas, however, several other local races are worth watching in terms of what they indicate about potential cooperation between the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), the pan-Blue-leaning third party, as well as internal dynamics within the KMT.

In Chiayi City, former legislator Chang Chi-kai is running as the TPP’s candidate, but with the backing of the KMT after winning a primary. However, he recently suffered a scandal after being caught on camera publicly urinating in a bush while on the campaign trail, and faces tough competition from DPP candidate Wang Mei-hui, a local politician who rose up through the Chiayi City Council.

In Hsinchu City, the TPP and KMT are jointly backing Ann Kao, who is actually running as an independent after leaving the TPP because of corruption charges that were later dismissed. Kao is often still perceived as TPP-affiliated – even if she has used the KMT’s blue as a campaign color in the current race. Kao is popular despite having previously faced legal charges involving embezzlement of public funds, of which she was later acquitted, and is expected to triumph against DPP opponent Chuang Ching-cheng.

The TPP and KMT are cooperating in some areas, while competing in others. The two parties officially suspended cooperation after failing to come to an agreement about who to run in Zhubei, which is the administrative capital of Hsinchu County.

Some KMT heavyweights, such as political commentator Jaw Shaw-kong and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an, have campaigned for the TPP in Zhubei. It is possible that Jaw and Chiang are chafing against party discipline set by KMT chair Cheng Li-wun.

For Chiang specifically, he may need the support of the TPP in order to maintain control of Taipei. Chiang has made frequent public appearances with members and affiliates of TPP – including acting party chair Huang Kuo-chang and well-known streamer Holger Chen – as part of his efforts to boost his standing in the Taipei mayor’s race.

The TPP’s Huang originally sought run as the New Taipei mayoral candidate of pan-Blue camp, but he eventually stepped aside in favor of Lee Shu-chuan. Lee’s poor performance since then likely stings. Huang may continue to seek an alliance with the KMT in the hopes that he is given another shot to run for a political position down the line. Huang currently holds no formal office.

If the 2026 local elections are expected to set the stage for 2028 elections, Cheng Li-wun is also thought to harbor presidential ambitions. Public perceptions of her as starkly pro-unification would make her a risky candidate for the KMT, however, and if the party does poorly in the 2026 local elections, she will face pressure to resign – something that rivals within the party would like to see. As such, the 2026 elections will also impact Cheng’s current standing within the KMT.

Local elections in Taiwan are primarily about local issues, or constituents’ choice of preferred political candidate. The rise of the “Ocean Current” phenomenon is an example – Shen’s appeal to the public has seen him doubling down on calls for good governance and policy expertise.

But the cross-strait dimension can intrude at times into local races. For example, a recent event held by KMT heavyweights – including former Taipei mayoral candidate Ting Shou-chung, 1992 Consensus architect Su Chi, and former majority speaker Wang Jin-pyng – provoked controversy because it set out a ten-year plan for unifying Taiwan and China. The plan discussed a shared economy in 2030, a joint currency in 2032, and talks on unification under frameworks including “One Country, Two Systems” by 2036. The controversy about this plan has led the KMT headquarters to distance itself from the notion.

It remains to be seen whether other controversies emerge before the voting on November 28. Whatever the result, these local races will set the stage for national elections, in terms of who emerges as potential frontrunners for future races.
